items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A computer-generated environment in which people interact, such as an online game world or a metaverse platform"?
options: data sovereignty
cyberspace
feedback loop
virtual space
items.answer: virtual space
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of virtual space.

items.stem: Briefly explain why physical place still matters in digital society.
items.answer: Infrastructure (cables, data centres, towers) is physically located; connectivity and speed vary by location (urban/rural), and national laws apply where users and servers are, so place shapes digital experience.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Infrastructure (cables, data centres, towers) is physically located; connectivity and speed vary by location (urban/rural), and national laws apply where users and servers are, so place shapes digital experience. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Alessia writes: "Being online means everyone has equal access to the same internet." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Access differs by place: censorship, geo-blocking, network quality and cost mean users in different countries or regions experience different internets.
items.markingKey: Access differs by place: censorship, geo-blocking, network quality and cost mean users in different countries or regions experience different internets. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Data may flow freely, but it always lives somewhere – in a building, in a country, under a law."
— Report on data governance, think tank, 2022

Explain what the source suggests about the concept of space in digital society.
items.answer: Even though data seems placeless, it is stored in physical data centres in particular countries and is governed by their laws, so physical and legal space still shape digital systems.
items.markingKey: Even though data seems placeless, it is stored in physical data centres in particular countries and is governed by their laws, so physical and legal space still shape digital systems. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Using China's Great Firewall as an example, explain digital borders.
items.answer: China blocks many foreign services (Google, Facebook, YouTube, WhatsApp) and promotes domestic platforms such as WeChat and Baidu. The state builds a national digital space with its own platforms and rules, showing that cyberspace can be bordered like physical territory.
items.markingKey: Context (China blocks many foreign services (Google, Facebook, YouTube, WhatsApp) and promotes domestic platforms such as WeChat and Baidu.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the state builds a national digital space with its own platforms and rules, showing that cyberspace can be bordered like physical territory. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to digital borders.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Digital technology has made geographical location irrelevant."
items.answer: Digital technology reduces the importance of distance for some people and activities, but location still shapes access, rights and experience.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: remote work and online learning across borders; instant global communication and virtual events. Arguments against: infrastructure, cost and speed vary greatly by place; national laws, firewalls and geo-blocking; rural and low-income regions remain offline. Supported judgement: Digital technology reduces the importance of distance for some people and activities, but location still shapes access, rights and experience.

items.stem: Which satellite internet service was activated in Ukraine in 2022 to maintain connectivity during the war?
options: Starlink
OneWeb only
Project Loon
Iridium
items.answer: Starlink
items.markingKey: A. SpaceX Starlink terminals were shipped to Ukraine from late February 2022.

items.stem: Distinguish between a virtual space and a physical space.
items.answer: A physical space has material location and boundaries (a school, a city); a virtual space is a digital environment where interaction is mediated by software and can be accessed from anywhere with a connection.
items.markingKey: A physical space has material location and boundaries (a school, a city); a virtual space is a digital environment where interaction is mediated by software and can be accessed from anywhere with a connection. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"In the metaverse you will be able to teleport instantly as a hologram to be at the office without a commute."
— Mark Zuckerberg, founder's letter, October 2021

Explain how the source illustrates the idea of time-space compression.
items.answer: It claims virtual presence will make physical distance irrelevant (no commute, instant presence), compressing space and time through digital technology; it is also a promotional claim from a company investing heavily in the metaverse.
items.markingKey: It claims virtual presence will make physical distance irrelevant (no commute, instant presence), compressing space and time through digital technology; it is also a promotional claim from a company investing heavily in the metaverse. items.stem: Felix writes: "Data stored "in the cloud" is not located anywhere physical." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Cloud data is stored on servers in physical data centres in specific countries, subject to those countries' laws and energy use.
items.markingKey: Cloud data is stored on servers in physical data centres in specific countries, subject to those countries' laws and energy use. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse how one virtual space has changed the way a community interacts, and evaluate whether it complements or replaces physical space.
items.answer: E.g. Roblox/Minecraft for young people, VRChat, Discord communities, Fortnite events; analyse new interactions, economies, rules; evaluate complement vs replacement with evidence.
items.markingKey: E.g. Roblox/Minecraft for young people, VRChat, Discord communities, Fortnite events; analyse new interactions, economies, rules; evaluate complement vs replacement with evidence.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Feedback that counteracts a change and keeps a system stable, such as a thermostat switching heating off when a temperature is reached"?
options: deontology
feedback loop
time-space compression
negative feedback
items.answer: negative feedback
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of negative feedback.

items.stem: Distinguish between the environment of a system and a component of a system.
items.answer: A component is a part inside the system boundary that interacts with other parts (e.g. an algorithm, servers, users); the environment is outside the boundary but influences it (e.g. law, culture, economy).
items.markingKey: A component is a part inside the system boundary that interacts with other parts (e.g. an algorithm, servers, users); the environment is outside the boundary but influences it (e.g. law, culture, economy). items.stem: "Feedback loops in digital systems are always harmful." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Negative feedback can stabilise systems (e.g. WhatsApp forwarding limits slowing rumours; thermostats in smart homes), and positive feedback can spread useful content quickly.
items.markingKey: Negative feedback can stabilise systems (e.g. WhatsApp forwarding limits slowing rumours; thermostats in smart homes), and positive feedback can spread useful content quickly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"When we limited forwards, the number of forwarded messages on WhatsApp fell by 25%."
— WhatsApp blog post, 2019

Explain how the intervention described works as negative feedback.
items.answer: Limiting forwards adds friction to the sharing loop, reducing how quickly messages multiply; this counteracts the amplifying positive feedback of viral forwarding.
items.markingKey: Limiting forwards adds friction to the sharing loop, reducing how quickly messages multiply; this counteracts the amplifying positive feedback of viral forwarding. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Briefly describe the 2010 Flash Crash and explain what it reveals about emergent behaviour in systems.
items.answer: On 6 May 2010 the Dow Jones fell nearly 1,000 points in minutes and recovered within about half an hour; regulators linked it to a large automated sell order and interacting high-frequency trading algorithms. No single algorithm intended a crash, but their rapid interactions produced a system-wide collapse, illustrating emergence and interdependence.
items.markingKey: Context (On 6 May 2010 the Dow Jones fell nearly 1,000 points in minutes and recovered within about half an hour; regulators linked it to a large automated sell order and interacting high-frequency trading algorithms.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: no single algorithm intended a crash, but their rapid interactions produced a system-wide collapse, illustrating emergence and interdependence. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to emergent behaviour in systems.

items.stem: Using a systems approach, analyse one digital system you have studied, identifying its components, a feedback loop and an emergent effect.
items.answer: E.g. a recommendation system: components (users, content, algorithm, advertisers), feedback (engagement → more promotion), emergent effect (viral trends, polarisation); include environment (regulation). Reward clear system mapping and explanation.
items.markingKey: E.g. a recommendation system: components (users, content, algorithm, advertisers), feedback (engagement → more promotion), emergent effect (viral trends, polarisation); include environment (regulation). Reward clear system mapping and explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why emergent behaviour makes digital systems hard to control.
items.answer: Outcomes such as viral trends, market crashes or misinformation cascades arise from millions of interactions rather than one designer's decision, so they cannot be fully predicted or controlled by changing one component.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Outcomes such as viral trends, market crashes or misinformation cascades arise from millions of interactions rather than one designer's decision, so they cannot be fully predicted or controlled by changing one component. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe WhatsApp's forwarding limits and explain what it reveals about negative feedback in a system.
items.answer: After rumours spread on WhatsApp were linked to mob violence in India in 2018, WhatsApp limited forwarding (to five chats, then one chat for frequently forwarded messages in 2020). Adding friction slowed the amplifying loop of mass forwarding, showing how design changes can stabilise a system.
items.markingKey: Context (After rumours spread on WhatsApp were linked to mob violence in India in 2018, WhatsApp limited forwarding (to five chats, then one chat for frequently forwarded messages in 2020).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: adding friction slowed the amplifying loop of mass forwarding, showing how design changes can stabilise a system. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to negative feedback in a system.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Each trading algorithm did exactly what it was programmed to do. Together, they did something no one programmed."
— Financial journalist, commentary on the 2010 Flash Crash

Explain how the source illustrates the concept of emergent behaviour.
items.answer: The crash was not designed by any single program; it emerged from interactions among many algorithms, each behaving correctly, which is the definition of emergence.
items.markingKey: The crash was not designed by any single program; it emerged from interactions among many algorithms, each behaving correctly, which is the definition of emergence. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An ethical approach that asks what a person of good character (honest, fair, courageous) would do (associated with Aristotle)"?

virtue ethics
negative feedback
data localisation
items.answer: virtue ethics
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of virtue ethics.

items.stem: Explain the difference between deontology and consequentialism.
items.answer: Consequentialism judges an action by its outcomes (e.g. whether encryption backdoors prevent more harm than they cause); deontology judges it by whether it respects duties and rights (e.g. never deceiving users), regardless of outcomes.
items.markingKey: Consequentialism judges an action by its outcomes (e.g. whether encryption backdoors prevent more harm than they cause); deontology judges it by whether it respects duties and rights (e.g. never deceiving users), regardless of outcomes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "If a technology is legal, it must be ethical." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Legality and ethics differ: laws lag behind technology and differ by country (e.g. the sale of location data by brokers is legal in many places but raises serious ethical concerns).
items.markingKey: Legality and ethics differ: laws lag behind technology and differ by country (e.g. the sale of location data by brokers is legal in many places but raises serious ethical concerns). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Apple v FBI (2016) shows an ethical dilemma between security and privacy.
items.answer: The FBI obtained a court order asking Apple to create software to bypass security on the San Bernardino attacker's iPhone; Apple refused, and the FBI dropped the case after a third party unlocked the phone. A utilitarian case for access (investigating terrorism) conflicted with a duty-based and consequential argument against weakening security for all users.
items.markingKey: Context (The FBI obtained a court order asking Apple to create software to bypass security on the San Bernardino attacker's iPhone; Apple refused, and the FBI dropped the case after a third party unlocked the phone.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a utilitarian case for access (investigating terrorism) conflicted with a duty-based and consequential argument against weakening security for all users. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to an ethical dilemma between security and privacy.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"The government is asking Apple to hack our own users and undermine decades of security advancements that protect our customers."
— Tim Cook, "A Message to Our Customers", Apple, 16 February 2016

Identify the ethical argument used in the source and explain it.
items.answer: It is a rights/duty-based (and consequential) argument: Apple has a duty to protect customers' security; creating a backdoor would harm all users, so it should refuse even for a legitimate investigation.
items.markingKey: It is a rights/duty-based (and consequential) argument: Apple has a duty to protect customers' security; creating a backdoor would harm all users, so it should refuse even for a legitimate investigation. items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Technology companies should prioritise user privacy over law-enforcement requests."
items.answer: Companies should resist blanket weakening of security but cooperate with lawful, targeted and proportionate requests; the balance depends on safeguards and the legal system.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: strong encryption protects everyone, including against criminals and authoritarian states; backdoors cannot be limited to "good" actors. Supported judgement: Companies should resist blanket weakening of security but cooperate with lawful, targeted and proportionate requests; the balance depends on safeguards and the legal system.

items.stem: Apply two ethical frameworks to one digital dilemma you have studied and evaluate which provides the more convincing guidance.
items.answer: E.g. live facial recognition, end-to-end encryption, or children's use of social media; apply consequentialism (weigh benefits/harms) and deontology or virtue ethics (duties, rights, character); compare their conclusions and evaluate.
items.markingKey: E.g. live facial recognition, end-to-end encryption, or children's use of social media; apply consequentialism (weigh benefits/harms) and deontology or virtue ethics (duties, rights, character); compare their conclusions and evaluate.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a utilitarian and a deontologist might disagree about using facial recognition in public spaces.
items.answer: A utilitarian may support it if it catches more criminals than the harm caused; a deontologist may oppose it because it treats everyone as a suspect and violates a duty to respect privacy and consent, regardless of benefits.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Kantian ethics judges actions mainly by their consequences.
Reason (R): Kant argued that people must be treated as ends and never merely as means.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. Kant is deontological (duty-based), so A is false; R is a correct statement of the categorical imperative.

items.stem: With reference to COVID-19 contact-tracing apps, explain how it illustrates consequentialist reasoning about public health and privacy.

Governments weighed the health benefits of tracing against privacy harms, and design choices (decentralised vs centralised) changed that balance.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Data localisation laws protect citizens more than they harm them."
items.answer: Localisation can strengthen protection where strong local privacy law exists, but in states with weak rights it can increase surveillance; its value depends on governance.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that complex digital systems are now too interconnected to be safe.
items.answer: Interconnection creates real systemic risk, but it can be managed through redundancy, diversity of suppliers and regulation; "too interconnected to be safe" overstates it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: single failures cascade globally (CrowdStrike 2024); emergent behaviour (Flash Crash) is hard to predict. Arguments against: redundancy, circuit breakers and testing reduce risks; interconnection also allows rapid recovery and updates; most systems work reliably most of the time. Supported judgement: Interconnection creates real systemic risk, but it can be managed through redundancy, diversity of suppliers and regulation; "too interconnected to be safe" overstates it. items.stem: "Technology companies should prioritise user privacy over law-enforcement requests." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Companies should resist blanket weakening of security but cooperate with lawful, targeted and proportionate requests; the balance depends on safeguards and the legal system.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: strong encryption protects everyone, including against criminals and authoritarian states; backdoors cannot be limited to "good" actors. Arguments against: serious crimes (child abuse, terrorism) may go uninvestigated; democratic legal processes have legitimate authority. Supported judgement: Companies should resist blanket weakening of security but cooperate with lawful, targeted and proportionate requests; the balance depends on safeguards and the legal system. items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that digital technology has made geographical location irrelevant.
items.answer: Digital technology reduces the importance of distance for some people and activities, but location still shapes access, rights and experience.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: remote work and online learning across borders; instant global communication and virtual events. Arguments against: infrastructure, cost and speed vary greatly by place; national laws, firewalls and geo-blocking; rural and low-income regions remain offline. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "utilitarianism"?
options: The interconnected digital environment of networks, data and online interactions
Feedback that counteracts a change and keeps a system stable, such as a thermostat switching heating off when a temperature is reached
A consequentialist theory (Bentham, Mill) that the right action produces the greatest overall happiness or well-being
A situation in which competing values or duties conflict, so that every option involves some moral cost
items.answer: A consequentialist theory (Bentham, Mill) that the right action produces the greatest overall happiness or well-being
items.markingKey: C. "utilitarianism" is a consequentialist theory (Bentham, Mill) that the right action produces the greatest overall happiness or well-being.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "geo-blocking".
items.answer: Restricting access to online content based on the user's geographic location
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: restricting access to online content based on the user's geographic location. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "positive feedback"?
options: Feedback that amplifies a change, for example content that gets engagement being shown to more people and getting even more engagement
An ethical approach that judges actions by whether they follow moral duties or rules, regardless of consequences (associated with Immanuel Kant)
The interconnected digital environment of networks, data and online interactions
A consequentialist theory (Bentham, Mill) that the right action produces the greatest overall happiness or well-being
items.answer: Feedback that amplifies a change, for example content that gets engagement being shown to more people and getting even more engagement
items.markingKey: A. "positive feedback" is feedback that amplifies a change, for example content that gets engagement being shown to more people and getting even more engagement.

items.stem: Distinguish between deontology and consequentialism.
items.answer: Consequentialism judges an action by its outcomes (e.g. whether encryption backdoors prevent more harm than they cause); deontology judges it by whether it respects duties and rights (e.g. never deceiving users), regardless of outcomes.
items.markingKey: Consequentialism judges an action by its outcomes (e.g. whether encryption backdoors prevent more harm than they cause); deontology judges it by whether it respects duties and rights (e.g. never deceiving users), regardless of outcomes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a physical space and a virtual space.
items.answer: A physical space has material location and boundaries (a school, a city); a virtual space is a digital environment where interaction is mediated by software and can be accessed from anywhere with a connection.
items.markingKey: A physical space has material location and boundaries (a school, a city); a virtual space is a digital environment where interaction is mediated by software and can be accessed from anywhere with a connection. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a component of a system and the environment of a system.
items.answer: A component is a part inside the system boundary that interacts with other parts (e.g. an algorithm, servers, users); the environment is outside the boundary but influences it (e.g. law, culture, economy).
items.markingKey: A component is a part inside the system boundary that interacts with other parts (e.g. an algorithm, servers, users); the environment is outside the boundary but influences it (e.g. law, culture, economy). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Utilitarianism always protects individual privacy." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Utilitarianism can justify sacrificing an individual's privacy if the total benefit (e.g. public health tracking) outweighs the harm; rights-based approaches give stronger protection.
items.markingKey: Utilitarianism can justify sacrificing an individual's privacy if the total benefit (e.g. public health tracking) outweighs the harm; rights-based approaches give stronger protection. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Being online means everyone has equal access to the same internet." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Access differs by place: censorship, geo-blocking, network quality and cost mean users in different countries or regions experience different internets.
items.markingKey: Access differs by place: censorship, geo-blocking, network quality and cost mean users in different countries or regions experience different internets. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why thinking in systems helps analyse the impacts of a digital technology.
items.answer: A systems view looks at components, interactions, feedback and environment, so it reveals indirect and unintended effects (e.g. ride-hailing affecting congestion, public transport and labour law) that a focus on the device alone would miss.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A systems view looks at components, interactions, feedback and environment, so it reveals indirect and unintended effects (e.g. ride-hailing affecting congestion, public transport and labour law) that a focus on the device alone would miss. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe the Cambridge Analytica scandal (2018) and explain what it reveals about deontological ethics and consent.
items.answer: Data from up to 87 million Facebook users were harvested through a personality-quiz app built by Aleksandr Kogan and used for political profiling. Users (and their friends) were used as means to political ends without informed consent, which Kantian ethics condemns regardless of any benefits.
items.markingKey: Context (Data from up to 87 million Facebook users were harvested through a personality-quiz app built by Aleksandr Kogan and used for political profiling.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: users (and their friends) were used as means to political ends without informed consent, which Kantian ethics condemns regardless of any benefits. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to deontological ethics and consent.

items.stem: Briefly describe China's Great Firewall and explain what it reveals about digital borders.
items.answer: China blocks many foreign services (Google, Facebook, YouTube, WhatsApp) and promotes domestic platforms such as WeChat and Baidu. The state builds a national digital space with its own platforms and rules, showing that cyberspace can be bordered like physical territory.
items.markingKey: Context (China blocks many foreign services (Google, Facebook, YouTube, WhatsApp) and promotes domestic platforms such as WeChat and Baidu.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Kwame writes: "Feedback loops in digital systems are always harmful." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Negative feedback can stabilise systems (e.g. WhatsApp forwarding limits slowing rumours; thermostats in smart homes), and positive feedback can spread useful content quickly.
items.markingKey: Negative feedback can stabilise systems (e.g. WhatsApp forwarding limits slowing rumours; thermostats in smart homes), and positive feedback can spread useful content quickly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Act in such a way that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end and never merely as a means."
— Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785)

Explain how this principle could be applied to targeted advertising based on personal data.
items.answer: Using people's data to manipulate their choices without informed consent treats them merely as a means to profit; Kant's principle would require transparency and genuine consent, treating users as rational agents.
items.markingKey: Using people's data to manipulate their choices without informed consent treats them merely as a means to profit; Kant's principle would require transparency and genuine consent, treating users as rational agents. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: "Data stored "in the cloud" is not located anywhere physical." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Cloud data is stored on servers in physical data centres in specific countries, subject to those countries' laws and energy use.
items.markingKey: Cloud data is stored on servers in physical data centres in specific countries, subject to those countries' laws and energy use. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "If each part of a system works correctly, the whole system will behave as intended." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Interactions between correctly working parts can produce emergent, unintended behaviour (e.g. trading algorithms each following rules but together causing the 2010 Flash Crash).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Complex digital systems are now too interconnected to be safe."
items.answer: Interconnection creates real systemic risk, but it can be managed through redundancy, diversity of suppliers and regulation; "too interconnected to be safe" overstates it.

items.stem: "Consequentialism is the most useful ethical framework for judging new digital technologies." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Consequentialism is valuable for weighing large-scale impacts, but it should be combined with rights-based constraints so minorities are not sacrificed for aggregate gains.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that data localisation laws protect citizens more than they harm them.
items.answer: Localisation can strengthen protection where strong local privacy law exists, but in states with weak rights it can increase surveillance; its value depends on governance.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: data subject to local privacy law and courts; protection from foreign surveillance; support local industry.
